Anharmonic vs. relaxational sound damping in glasses:
II. Vitreous silica

René Vacher, Eric Courtens, and Marie Foret Affiliation: Groupe de Physique des Verres et Spectroscopies, LCVN, UMR CNRS 5587,
Université Montpellier II, F-34095 Montpellier Cedex 5, France
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The temperature dependence of the frequency dispersion in the sound velocity and damping of vitreous silica is reanalyzed. Thermally activated relaxation accounts for the sound attenuation observed above 10 K at sonic and ultrasonic frequencies. Its extrapolation to the hypersonic regime reveals that the anharmonic coupling to the thermal bath becomes important in Brillouin-scattering measurements. At 35 GHz and room temperature, the damping due to this anharmonicity is found to be nearly twice that produced by thermally activated relaxation. The analysis also reveals a sizeable velocity increase with temperature which is not related with sound dispersion. A possible explanation is that silica experiences a gradual structural change that already starts well below room temperature.

I Introduction

In the first paper of this series (I), the hypersonic attenuation of highly densified silica glass, dd-SiO2, was investigated. It was found that in that material the damping of hypersound is completely dominated by its anharmonic interaction with the thermally dominant modes. In the present paper we consider the corresponding situation in usual vitreous silica, vv-SiO2, for which a large quantity of high quality data is already available in the literature. In the early 1950’s, ultrasonic absorption peaks in function of the temperature TT were first observed in vv-SiO2. These were described by Anderson and Bömmel in terms of a phenomenological Maxwell model [1]. Following the discovery of the key role played by two-level systems (TLS) in producing the anomalous thermal properties of glasses [2, 3], it became clear that these should also be invoked in the description of acoustic relaxation. A theory including both resonant and relaxational sound damping produced by tunneling was developed by Jäckle [4]. It was then extended to higher temperatures by including in the description the classical jumps over the energy barrier separating the wells of TLS [5]. The presently accepted model for thermally activated relaxation (TAR) includes a distribution of asymmetric double-well potentials, as discussed by Gilroy and Phillips [6].

The simple extrapolation of this behavior to GHz frequencies, i.e. to the hypersonic regime, has sometimes been presented as an appropriate description of the observed phenomena, e.g. in [7, 8] or [9]. However, it has also been recognized that TAR might not always be sufficient to account for sound dispersion and damping. A specific example has been discussed in the case of vitreous germania, GeO2 [10]. The results presented in (I) strongly suggest that vv-SiO2 should be an excellent candidate to search for a possible anharmonic contribution to the hypersonic attenuation.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section II the phenomenology of TAR is reviewed to formulate a description that can reasonably be extrapolated to sufficiently high-TT and to Brillouin-scattering frequencies. In Section III this formalism is applied to available high quality sonic and ultrasonic data on vv-SiO2, covering more than four orders of magnitude in the frequency ν\nu. The model parameters that are thus extracted are then used in Section IV to estimate the TAR contributions to both velocity dispersion and damping at Brillouin-scattering frequencies. The anharmonic contribution can then be extracted from the total signal. It is analyzed in terms of a mean thermal mode relaxation time τth\tau_{\rm th} in Section V. Interestingly, this time is found to be about an order of magnitude longer than that of densified silica glass, dd-SiO2. Section VI presents a synthesis of the above analysis for the entire range of ν\nu, from ultrasonic to Brillouin-scattering frequencies. A part of that analysis concerns the velocity changes with TT. We find an anomalous increase of the bare velocity v∞v_{\infty} with TT, nearly the same in vv-SiO2 and dd-SiO2. This unrelaxed velocity, v∞v_{\infty}, is obtained after subtraction of the velocity changes produced by both thermally activated relaxation and anharmonicity. The TT-dependence of v∞v_{\infty} suggests that silica experiences a progressive structural change with increasing TT. Section VII is a discussion, which mentions the crossovers between the various frequency regimes, considers the suitability of power laws for the description of the dependence of the damping on ν\nu, and evoques possible extension to other glasses.

II The phenomenology of thermally activated relaxation

We consider an assembly of defects represented by double-well potentials that are separated by barriers of height VV and whose depths differ by the asymmetry Δ\Delta. The energies VV and Δ\Delta are randomly distributed according to a distribution P⁡(Δ,V)​d​Δ​d​VP(\Delta,V)\>d\Delta\>dV to be discussed below. The system is thought to hop continuously between the wells. The energy difference between the wells is coupled to the strain 𝐞\bf e of a sound wave of angular frequency Ω≡2​π​ν\Omega\equiv 2\pi\,\nu by a deformation potential γ=12​∂Δ/∂e\gamma={\scriptstyle\frac{1}{2}}\partial\Delta/\partial e. Owing to the delayed energy exchanged in hopping, this produces the dissipation of the sound wave. This situation has been described in great details elsewhere [5, 6, 11, 12]. To an excellent approximation, it leads to a relaxational contribution to the internal friction given by

Qrel−1=γ2ρ​v2​T​∫−∞∞d​Δ​∫0∞d​V​P​(Δ,V)​sech2​Δ2​T​Ω​τ1+Ω2​τ2.Q_{\rm rel}^{-1}\;=\;\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\rho v^{2}T}\;\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\Delta\;\int_{0}^{\infty}dV\;P(\Delta,V)\;{\rm sech}^{2}\frac{\Delta}{2T}\;\frac{\Omega\tau}{1+\Omega^{2}\tau^{2}}\;\;. (1​a)

In this expression, ρ\rho is the material density, vv is the velocity of sound, and TT is in energy units. We remark that both γ\gamma and vv depend on the polarization of the acoustic wave, longitudinal (LA) or transverse (TA). In this writing, VV is restricted to positive values while the distribution is symmetric in Δ\Delta. We also note that P⁡(Δ,V)​d​Δ​d​VP(\Delta,V)\>d\Delta\>dV is a density, i.e. a number per unit volume. The associated velocity change, which follows from the Kramers-Kronig relation, is given by

(δ​vv)rel=−12γ2ρ​v2​T∫−∞∞dΔ∫0∞dVP(Δ,V)sech2Δ2​T11+Ω2​τ2.\left(\frac{\delta v}{v}\right)_{\rm rel}\;=\;-\frac{1}{2}\;\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\rho v^{2}T}\;\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\Delta\;\int_{0}^{\infty}dV\;P(\Delta,V)\;{\rm sech}^{2}\frac{\Delta}{2T}\;\frac{1}{1+\Omega^{2}\tau^{2}}\;\;. (1​b)

In these equations, τ\tau is the relaxation time for hopping within the double well. It is given by

τ=τ0​exp​VT​sech​Δ2​T,\tau\;=\;\tau_{0}\;{\rm exp}\,\frac{V}{T}\;{\rm sech}\,\frac{\Delta}{2T}\;\;, (2)

where τ0\tau_{0} is the inverse of an attempt frequency, as shown in detail e.g. in [12].

The key in applying these expressions is to use a reasonable distribution P⁡(Δ,V)P(\Delta,V). For small Δ\Delta and VV the distribution is often replaced by a constant P¯\bar{P}. This is suggested by the TT-dependence of the specific heat at low TT which only probes low values of Δ\Delta and VV [13]. Of course, a constant P¯\bar{P} cannot be extended to high values of Δ\Delta and VV as this leads to a diverging integral density of defects which is unphysical. A reasonable guess for P⁡(Δ,V)P(\Delta,V) can be obtained with the help of the soft-potential model (SPM) [14]. That model is characterized by a distribution of random dimensionless cubic and quadratic coefficients, ξ\xi and η\eta respectively, by an energy scale of the potential ℰ0{\cal E}_{0}, and by a characteristic cross-over energy W≪ℰ0W\ll{\cal E}_{0} [14]. We are only interested here in the region η<0\eta<0 with 1≫|η|≫ξ21\gg|\eta|\gg\xi^{2} which gives double wells with barriers centered at the origin of the soft mode coordinate xx. As shown in [15], owing to the latter choice, the variables ξ\xi and η\eta are not statistically independent. This leads to a sea-gull singularity in their distribution, P⁡(ξ,η)=12​|η|​𝒫0​(ξ,η)P(\xi,\eta)={\scriptstyle\frac{1}{2}}|\eta|{\cal P}_{0}(\xi,\eta), where 𝒫0​(ξ,η){\cal P}_{0}(\xi,\eta) is finite near the origin. For the range of values of interest here, one has Δ=ℰ0​12​ξ​|η|3/2\Delta={\cal E}_{0}{\scriptstyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}\xi|\eta|^{3/2} and V=14​ℰ0​|η|2V={\scriptstyle\frac{1}{4}}{\cal E}_{0}|\eta|^{2}. The deformation potential of the SPM is also function of |η||\eta| with γSPM2∝|η|\gamma_{\rm SPM}^{2}\propto|\eta| as defined in [16] and further explained in [17]. The terms γ2​P​(Δ,V)​d​Δ​d​V\gamma^{2}P(\Delta,V)\,d\Delta\,dV of (1aa) are transformed into γSPM2​P​(ξ,η)​d​ξ​d​η\gamma_{\rm SPM}^{2}P(\xi,\eta)\,d\xi\,d\eta in the SPM. Using the Jacobian |∂(Δ,V)/∂(ξ,η)|=ℰ02​12​2​|η|5/2|\partial(\Delta,V)/\partial(\xi,\eta)|={\cal E}_{0}^{2}{\scriptstyle\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}}|\eta|^{5/2}, one finds that P(Δ,V)∝V−1/4𝒫0(ξ,η)P(\Delta,V)\propto V^{-1/4}{\cal P}_{0}(\xi,\eta) [16]. This was already used by Keil et al. [18] who selected a distribution P⁡(V)P(V) proportional to V−ζV^{-\zeta} times a gaussian. These authors experimentally found that indeed ζ\zeta is very near 1/4 in the case of silica.

For convenience, and for lack of different compelling indications, we assume that the distribution can be factored into

P⁡(Δ,V)=f⁡(Δ)​g​(V).P(\Delta,V)\;=\;f(\Delta)\;g(V)\;\;. (3)

For g⁡(V)g(V), inspired by [16] and [18], we use the normalized form

g⁡(V)=Ng​1V0​(VV0)−ζ​exp​(−12​V2V02).g(V)\;=\;N_{\rm g}\;\frac{1}{V_{0}}\;\left(\frac{V}{V_{0}}\right)^{-\zeta}{\rm exp}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{V^{2}}{V_{0}^{2}}\right)\;\;. (4​a)

Since ζ<1\zeta<1, this expression is integrable. The norm NgN_{\rm g} is selected so that g⁡(V)g(V) integrates to 1. This gives

Ng−1=∫0∞x−ζ​exp​(−12​x2)​𝑑x=Γ⁡(1−ζ)​U​(12−ζ,0).N_{\rm g}^{-1}\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{-\zeta}{\rm exp}(-{\scriptstyle\frac{1}{2}}x^{2})dx\;=\;\Gamma(1-\zeta)\;U({\scriptstyle\frac{1}{2}}-\zeta,0)\;\;. (4​b)

The function U⁡(a,0)U(a,0) is the parabolic cylinder function [19]. As explained in the following Section, our independent analysis of a collection of data larger than that used in [18] also leads to ζ\zeta very close to 1/4. This provides a solid support for this particular choice of g⁡(V)g(V). For f⁡(Δ)f(\Delta) we use a simple gaussian, rather similar to the gaussian cut-off of the linear asymmetry coefficient D1D_{1} used by Gil et al. [20]. Indeed, D1∝ξ|η|∝ΔV−1/4D_{1}\propto\xi|\eta|\propto\Delta V^{-1/4}, so that a gaussian in D1D_{1} is very close to one in Δ\Delta, the power of VV connecting the two variables being quite small. This functional form for f⁡(Δ)f(\Delta) was already employed succesfully by Bonnet [21]. It is written

f⁡(Δ)=Nf​f0​exp​(−12​Δ2ΔC2),f(\Delta)\;=\;N_{\rm f}\>f_{0}\>{\rm exp}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\Delta^{2}}{\Delta_{\rm C}^{2}}\right)\;\;, (5​a)

where f0f_{0} is defined by the normalization condition that the integral of f⁡(Δ)f(\Delta) equals f0​V0f_{0}V_{0}. The norm NfN_{\rm f} is then dimensionless and given by

Nf−1=∫−∞∞exp⁡(−12​δ2​x2)​𝑑x=2​π/δ,N_{\rm f}^{-1}\;=\;\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}{\rm exp}(-{\scriptstyle\frac{1}{2}}\delta^{2}x^{2})\,dx\;=\;\sqrt{2\pi}/\delta\;\;, (5​b)

δ≡V0/ΔC,\delta\;\equiv\;V_{0}/\Delta_{\rm C}\;\;, (6)

N≡∫−∞∞d​Δ​∫0∞d​V​P​(Δ,V)=f0​V0.N\;\equiv\;\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\Delta\;\int_{0}^{\infty}dV\;P(\Delta,V)\;=\;f_{0}V_{0}\;\;. (7)

To complete the calculation, we now introduce (4) and (5) into (1), and use (2). In performing the integrals in (1), we make the same approximation as in [6] that sech(Δ/2​T\Delta/2T) is replaced by 1 for |Δ|< 2​T|\Delta|\;<\;2T and by zero otherwise. This eliminates the sech factors in (1) and (2) and simply replaces the limits of integration on Δ\Delta by ±2​T\pm 2T. It is convenient to define a dimensionless constant

𝒞≡γ2​f0​Ng/ρ​v2.{\cal C}\;\equiv\;\gamma^{2}f_{0}N_{\rm g}/\rho v^{2}\;\;. (8)

One obtains

(δ​vv)rel=−12𝒞Φ(2​TΔC)1T∫0∞(VV0)−ζexp(−12V2V02)11+Ω2​τ02​exp​(2​V/T)dV,\left(\frac{\delta v}{v}\right)_{\rm rel}\;=\;-\frac{1}{2}\;{\cal C}\>\Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}\,T}{\Delta_{\rm C}}\right)\>\frac{1}{T}\>\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{V}{V_{0}}\right)^{-\zeta}{\rm exp}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{V^{2}}{V_{0}^{2}}\right)\;\frac{1}{1+\Omega^{2}\tau_{0}^{2}\>{\rm exp}(2V/T)}\>dV\;\;, (9​b)

Given the distribution (4), one cannot strictly define P¯\bar{P}, but this does not prevent defining CC in a consistent manner [16]. We calculate this for ζ=14\zeta={\scriptstyle\frac{1}{4}}. We use γSPM2=12​Λ2​|η|\gamma_{\rm SPM}^{2}={\scriptstyle\frac{1}{2}}\Lambda^{2}|\eta| and C=Λ2​𝒫0​ηL7/2/W​ρ​v2C=\Lambda^{2}{\cal P}_{0}\,\eta_{\rm L}^{7/2}\,/\,W\rho v^{2} from [16], where ηL2≡W/ℰ0\eta_{\rm L}^{2}\equiv W/{\cal E}_{0}. C=2π​W3/4​V01/4ΔC​𝒞.C\;=\;\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\;\frac{W^{3/4}V_{0}^{1/4}}{\Delta_{\rm C}}\;{\cal C}\;\;. (11)

Information on the numerical handling of Eqs. (9) and our choice of suitable fitting parameters are found in Appendix A.

III Analysis of sonic and ultrasonic relaxational data

It is generally agreed that sonic or ultrasonic damping at temperatures above ∼10\sim 10 K is dominated by thermally activated relaxation. To obtain the model parameters V0V_{0}, ΔC\Delta_{\rm C}, and τ0\tau_{0} entering Eqs.(9)\;(9), it is necessary to analyze acoustic results over a sufficiently large range of frequencies ν\nu, this up to high ultrasonic frequencies. It implies comparing data from various sources and generally acquired with different measurement techniques. TAR leads to a peak in Qrel−1Q_{\rm rel}^{-1} as observed by Anderson and Bömmel in ultrasonic pulse-echo measurements [1]. These authors report precise data obtained on the TA-mode of vitreous silica at ν=20\nu=20 MHz. This is one of the curves that will be used for our analysis, as displayed in Fig. 1\;1. Other high-frequency data were measured using the Bragg diffraction of light, [23] in a set-up similar to the original Debye-Sears experiment [24]. Damping results at ν≃200\nu\simeq 200 MHz on both LA- and TA-modes have been obtained in that manner [23]. From these, and from results presented in [25], it is clear that LA- and TA-modes lead to identical Q−1Q^{-1} peak shapes. This implies that similar distributions of defects are active in the damping of all acoustic waves, independently from their polarizations. We use the data on the LA-mode at 207 MHz from [23], also shown in Fig. 1\>1. The independence from polarization allows including in the evaluation sonic frequency results acquired on macroscopic vibrational modes, such as in vibrating reed measurements. We use the data at ν=11.4\nu=11.4 kHz of Classen, as reported in [12]. This curve is also displayed in Fig. 1\>1. Results at intermediate frequencies were collected using composite oscillators, at 660 kHz on the LA-mode in [6], and at 180 kHz on a torsional mode in [18]. As remarked in [18], this particular method can easily lead to instrumental background-loss contributions. This might have been the case in [6], as suggested from data on other glasses presented by the same authors in [26] which show long absorption tails at high TT. This notion is also supported by fits that are explained below. Hence, it is the 180 kHz data from [18] which is included in Fig. 1\;1. With these four curves, the analysed data covers more than four decades in ν\nu with a nearly linear progression in log​ν{\rm log}\,\nu.

The curves shown in Fig. 1\;1 have been simultaneously adjusted to Eq.(9​a)\;(9a), allowing for each measurement an independent coupling parameter 𝒞\cal C. In the Marquardt-Levenberg routine used to this effect, the weights have been adjusted so that each curve had approximately the same weight, independently from the number of data points at each particular frequency. The excellent results of this fit, with ζ\zeta fixed at 1/4, are illustrated by the solid lines in Fig. 1\;1. The distribution parameters corresponding to these lines are V0=659±19V_{0}=659\pm 19 K, log10​τ0=−12.2±0.14{\rm log}_{10}\tau_{0}=-12.2\pm 0.14 with τ0\tau_{0} in seconds, and V0/ΔC=8.2±0.6V_{0}/\Delta_{\rm C}=8.2\pm 0.6. If the same fit is repeated with ζ\zeta free, one finds ζ=0.28±0.03\zeta=0.28\pm 0.03, and similar values for the other parameters: V0=667±21V_{0}=667\pm 21 K, log10​τ0=−12.2±0.18{\rm log}_{10}\tau_{0}=-12.2\pm 0.18, and V0/ΔC=7.7±0.7V_{0}/\Delta_{\rm C}=7.7\pm 0.7. This shows that the distribution g⁡(V)g(V) suggested by the SPM is very adequate indeed. It also shows that ζ\zeta can be fixed at 1/4, which will be done for the rest of this paper. The rather high value obtained for V0/ΔCV_{0}/\Delta_{\rm C} emphasizes that one should not neglect the cut-off in the asymmetry distribution. We return to this point below.

Our analysis reveals a certain difficulty in comparing the absolute size of the various curves. This can be related to some extent to the different polarizations of the waves in these measurements, or also to a small part to the different qualities of the silica samples employed. However, it seems more likely that it arises to a large part from calibration inaccuracies in some of these measurements. Indeed, discrepancies in the size of Q−1Q^{-1} are directly observed in comparing literature reports, for example for the TA-waves at 20 MHz in [1] and [25]. The difficulty is also seen in comparing the LA to TA values of Q−1Q^{-1} in [23] and in [25]. While in the former case it is the attenuations that have the same amplitudes for both LA and TA, in the latter it is the internal frictions which are practically the same for both polarizations. This cannot be reconciled as attenuation and friction differ by a factor proportional to the sound velocity, and the latter is ≃5900\simeq 5900 m/s for LA and ≃3800\simeq 3800 m/s for TA-waves at low TT. We also observed that the results at 660 kHz in [6] are fitted extremely well with the same model parameters, provided one allows for a relatively small constant background contribution to Q−1Q^{-1}, equal to 0.1×10−30.1\times 10^{-3}. The values of 𝒞\cal C obtained for these various measurements range then from 1.1×10−31.1\times 10^{-3} in the case of [6] to 1.8×10−31.8\times 10^{-3} for [1]. These variations in 𝒞\cal C do not seem correlated to either the measuring frequency or the wave polarization, which is another reason to suspect calibration difficulties.

It is necessary to obtain a more reliable value of 𝒞\cal C to analyze the Brillouin scattering data in the following Section. To this effect we remark that velocity measurements are generally both accurate and precise, allowing to follow small changes in δ​v/v\delta v/v with excellent accuracy. We use two measurements of the LA-wave velocity, one at 660 kHz from [6] and the other at 6.8 MHz from [23]. The experimental values (δ​v/v)exp(\delta v/v)_{\rm exp} are shown in Fig. 2\>2, together with continuous lines marked (δ​v/v)rel(\delta v/v)_{\rm rel}. These are calculated from the relaxation equation (9​b)(9b) using the above values of V0V_{0}, ΔC\Delta_{\rm C}, and τ0\tau_{0}, together with 𝒞=1.4×10−3{\cal C}=1.4\times 10^{-3}. With the latter value, the dip around 50 K is completely accounted for. This is emphasized by the difference (δ​v/v)exp−(δ​v/v)rel(\delta v/v)_{\rm exp}-(\delta v/v)_{\rm rel} also shown in Fig. 2\;2. Hence, we adopt for the following the coupling constant 𝒞=1.4×10−3{\cal C}=1.4\times 10^{-3} which happens to fall within the range of values obtained by fitting the various Q−1Q^{-1} curves discussed above.

We now return to the small cut-off value ΔC≃80\Delta_{\rm C}\simeq 80 K which we obtained. This aspect has mostly been ignored by other workers. It was shown in [21] that it is necessary to include a cut-off to obtain a good fit to the high-TT tails in Fig. 1. For example, forcing ΔC=V0\Delta_{\rm C}=V_{0}, the quality of the fits degrades appreciably above ∼70\sim 70 K, especially for the highest ν\nu curve. More importantly, the calculated values of (δ​v/v)rel(\delta v/v)_{\rm rel} are then much too large to account properly for the dip around 60 K observed in Fig. 2. Obviously, by the virtue of the Kramers-Kronig transform, (δ​v/v)rel(\delta v/v)_{\rm rel} integrates over a large part of the distribution, which is the reason for this problem. One might wish to gain an intuitive picture of why ΔC\Delta_{\rm C} can be so much smaller than V0V_{0}. To this effect, one can consider the models of TAR drawn in Fig. 2 of [27]. We take as simplest examples model A, in which the two Si atoms of a Si−-O−-Si bond are too close, and model B, in which they are too far apart. In either case, a double well potential for the connecting oxygen results with a barrier height VV that comes mainly from the separation of the two Si. This barrier can thus be quite high. On the other hand, the asymmetry is produced by the difference in the wider environment of the two wells. In a hard glass, one might expect that these environments, which are dictated by the minimization of the energy, can be mostly quite similar. From these considerations, one intuitively anticipates that the ratio V0/ΔCV_{0}/\Delta_{\rm C} might depend significantly on the particular glass.

Finally, we remark that the temperature TmaxT_{\rm max} of the peak positions in Fig. 1\;1 depends linearly on lnΩ\,\Omega. A similar observation was already made in [27]. This typical Arrhenius behavior supports TAR as the principal relaxation mechanism to describe Fig. 1\;1, as opposed for example to incoherent tunneling that would lead to Tmax∝ΩT_{\rm max}\propto\sqrt{\Omega} as seen from Eq. (2.95) of [28].

IV Analysis of Brillouin scattering results

High-resolution Brillouin scattering measurements of the temperature dependence of the LA-linewidth of vitreous silica have been reported in [29] and [12]. Both experiments were performed near backscattering and below room TT, using as exciting radiation the blue argon-laser line at λL=488\lambda_{\rm L}=488 nm. Measurements above room TT are reported in [30]. These were performed at λL=514\lambda_{\rm L}=514 nm. The Brillouin frequency shifts νB\nu_{\rm B} from [29] and [30], the latter rescaled to λL=488\lambda_{\rm L}=488 nm, are displayed in Fig.(3​a)\;(3a) over the entire range of TT.

The frequency widths extracted from the Brillouin peaks in [29] and [30], after correction for the instrumental broadening, have been converted to internal friction as shown in Fig.(3​b)\;(3b). The internal friction reported by Tielbürger et al. in [12] is also shown on the same figure. One notices the remarkable agreement between these two independent determinations. It emphasizes that Brillouin scattering gives an absolute measurement of Q−1Q^{-1}, independent from calibrations, since it suffices to take the ratio of the Brillouin full-width to the Brillouin shift to extract Q−1Q^{-1}. This statement of course assumes that the spectroscopy can be performed with the required resolution, and in particular that the broadening produced by the finite collection aperture can be made sufficiently small.

Also shown in Fig.(3​b)\;(3b) is the curve Qrel−1Q_{\rm rel}^{-1} calculated with Eq.(9​a)\;(9a) for ν=35\nu=35 GHz and with the parameters determined in Section III. It is evident that at Brillouin frequencies TAR cannot account for the entire internal friction. The value 𝒞≃1.4×10−3{\cal C}\simeq 1.4\times 10^{-3} is confirmed by the Brillouin velocity results explained below. However, even if one would allow oneself to arbitrarily double the coupling constant 𝒞\cal C, the line in Fig. 3​(b)\;3(b) would still not superpose the data points. In particular the peak in Qrel−1Q_{\rm rel}^{-1} occurs at a lower TT-value than the peak in the observed Q−1Q^{-1}. The difference between the two curves is attributed to its largest part to the anharmonic coupling of the LA-waves with the thermally excited vibrational modes, as reported in (I) for densified silica glass.

The velocities are extracted from the Brillouin frequencies νB\nu_{\rm B} of Fig.(3​a)\;(3a) using v=λL​νB/ 2​n​sin​θ2v=\lambda_{\rm L}\nu_{\rm B}\,/\,2n\,{\rm sin}\,{\frac{\theta}{2}}, where nn is the refractive index and θ\theta is the internal scattering angle, here close to 180∘180^{\circ}. To derive precise values on v⁡(T)v(T), it is necessary to know n⁡(T)n(T) with an equal precision. This information has been derived from [31]. The results below 300 K are shown in Fig. 4, together with the velocities at 6.8 MHz from [23].

The relative changes reported in [6] have also been converted back to velocities using v0=5888v_{0}=5888 m/s. Subtracting from all three curves the (δ​v)rel(\delta v)_{\rm rel} calculated from Eq.(9​b)\;(9b), one observes that below 150 K all the data collapse quite well. This confirms that the value of 𝒞\cal C is also correct at Brillouin frequencies. It also emphasizes that the ν\nu-dependence in the depth of the dip around 70 K is well predicted by TAR. As explained in Section VIB, the velocity changes that are produced by the anharmonicity, (δ​v)anh(\delta v)_{\rm anh}, show little dispersion compared to the large dispersion in (δ​v)rel(\delta v)_{\rm rel}. Hence, they do not modify the above conclusion.

Figure 5 shows the difference between the experimental internal friction and the calculated TAR contribution. Similarly to the results on dd-SiO2 in (I), there is a region where the signal falls rapidly with decreasing TT. However, it does not seem to fall to zero sufficiently fast. In spite of the large scatter in the experimental values, there is a hint for an additional contribution to Q−1Q^{-1} at low TT, in the region from ∼20\sim 20 to ∼60\sim 60 K.

At these hypersonic frequencies and temperatures, one can anticipate a contribution QTLS−1Q_{\rm TLS}^{-1} arising from the relaxation of two-level systems (TLS) by incoherent tunneling. Generally, QTLS−1​(T)Q_{\rm TLS}^{-1}(T) exhibits a plateau separating a regime Ω​τmin≫1\Omega\tau_{\rm min}\gg 1 at low T<T∼T<\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textstyle\sim}}{{T}} from Ω​τmin≪1\Omega\tau_{\rm min}\ll 1 at higher TT, as shown in [28] where τmin\tau_{\rm min} and T∼∝Ω1/3\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textstyle\sim}}{{T}}\propto\Omega^{1/3} are defined. The position, extent, and height of this plateau are Ω\Omega-dependent, as emphasized in Fig. 6 of [32]. According to [28], the extent of the plateau should shrink to zero at sufficiently high frequencies such that T∼>T∗\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textstyle\sim}}{{T}}>T^{*}, where T∗T^{*} is a frequency independent characteristic temperature marking the end of the plateau region. In vv-SiO2, it has been observed that T∗≃5T^{*}\simeq 5 K [12]. The plateau becomes then a hump slightly above T∼\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textstyle\sim}}{{T}}. As shown in [32], for ν=46\nu=46 MHz one should have T∼≃3\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textstyle\sim}}{{T}}\simeq 3 K. This value increases with Ω1/3\Omega^{1/3}, as confirmed from sound-damping data between 330 and 930 MHz [33], showing a shoulder on the low TT side of the TAR peak. Hence, at 35 GHz one expects T∼∼30\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textstyle\sim}}{{T}}\sim 30 K, giving a broad TLS hump centered around 40 K. QTLS−1∝T3Q_{\rm TLS}^{-1}\propto T^{3} below this hump, and QTLS−1∝T−1Q_{\rm TLS}^{-1}\propto T^{-1} above it [28]. Extrapolating the observations reported in [32] we posit

QTLS−1=1.3×10−3(30/T)3+(T/30)Q_{\rm TLS}^{-1}\;=\;\frac{1.3\times 10^{-3}}{(30/T)^{3}\,+\,(T/30)}\;\; (12)

as a rough estimate for this relatively small contribution to Q−1Q^{-1}. This curve, which peaks around 40 K, is shown in Fig. 5. The difference

Qanh−1=Q−1−Qrel−1−QTLS−1Q_{\rm anh}^{-1}\;=\;Q^{-1}\,-\,Q_{\rm rel}^{-1}\,-\,Q_{\rm TLS}^{-1}\;\; (13)

will be used below to analyse the anharmonic damping. Since there seems to be a small tunneling contribution QTLS−1Q_{\rm TLS}^{-1}, then there ought to be by the Kramers-Kronig relation a corresponding contribution (δ​v)TLS(\delta v)_{\rm TLS}. As shown in Eq. (2.96) of [28], this should produce at high-TT a frequency dependent term in T​ln​ΩT\,{\rm ln}\,\Omega. As shown in Appendix B, there are reasons to believe that it is this term that produces the difference in slopes indicated by short dashed lines in Fig. 4.

To conclude, we find a relatively large Qanh−1Q_{\rm anh}^{-1} at hypersonic frequencies. It is of the same order of magnitude as Qrel−1Q_{\rm rel}^{-1}. The small additional term QTLS−1Q_{\rm TLS}^{-1} that has been discussed above is a correction of minor importance compared to Qanh−1Q_{\rm anh}^{-1}, as obvious from Fig. 5.

V The thermal relaxation time

In the spirit of (I) we now analyze the anharmonic damping with the expression

Qanh−1=A​Ω​τth1+Ω2​τth2,Q_{\rm anh}^{-1}\;=\;A\;\frac{\Omega\tau_{\rm th}}{1+\Omega^{2}\tau_{\rm th}^{2}}\;\;, (14)

where τth\tau_{\rm th} is the mean lifetime of the thermal modes and A⁡(T)=γ2​Cv​T​v/2​ρ​vD3A(T)=\gamma^{2}C_{\rm v}Tv/2\rho v_{\rm D}^{3} is the prefactor given in Eq.(5​b)\;(5b) of (I), with CvC_{\rm v} the specific heat per unit volume and vDv_{\rm D} the Debye velocity. We remark that all quantities entering A⁡(T)A(T) are known, except for the mean-square average Grüneisen parameter γ2\gamma^{2}. Thus we can directly plot the quantity γ2​Qanh−1/A\gamma^{2}Q_{\rm anh}^{-1}/A as it is independent from γ2\gamma^{2}. The result obtained using the values Qanh−1Q_{\rm anh}^{-1} taken from Fig. 5 is drawn in Fig.(6​a)\;(6a).

Points below 60 K are not shown as the data is too noisy at low TT to be significant after division by A∝Cv​TA\propto C_{\rm v}T. This plot exhibits a peak for Ω​τth= 1\Omega\tau_{\rm th}\,=\,1. From the height of this peak one reads γ2≃3.6\gamma^{2}\simeq 3.6. With this determination, Eq. (14) can then be solved for Ω​τth\Omega\tau_{\rm th}, and thus for τth\tau_{\rm th}. The procedure is explained in Appendix C. The result is shown in Fig.(6​b)\;(6b). One observes that τth​(T)\tau_{\rm th}(T) is proportional to T−2T^{-2} over the main part of the data, from ∼100\sim 100 K to ∼300\sim 300 K. At higher TT, τth\tau_{\rm th} tapers off, while at lower TT there is a hint that τth​(T)\tau_{\rm th}(T) might diverge faster than in T−2T^{-2}. The solid line is a guide to the eye which is a sum of powers of TT. The same law is then used to trace the guide to the eye in Fig.(6​a)\;(6a).

In Fig.(6​b)\;(6b) we have traced for comparison the values of the relaxation time of the thermal modes for two other cases. Firstly, we observe that τth​(T)\tau_{\rm th}(T) obtained in (I) for densified silica glass, dd-SiO2, is substantially shorter than in vv-SiO2. However, it shows a very similar functional dependence on TT. Secondly, in order to deepen the understanding, we applied the same method of analysis to data on the LA-mode of X-cut crystal quartz, cc-SiO2. We used to this effect the attenuation coefficient measured by Bömmel and Dransfeld at 1 GHz [34]. At temperatures above 150 K, we completed these data using the width of the Brillouin line reported in [35]. These data were analyzed similarly to Fig.(6​a)\;(6a) leading to γ2≃0.95\gamma^{2}\simeq 0.95. The corresponding τth​(T)\tau_{\rm th}(T) is shown in Fig.(6​b)\;(6b). In this case, the line through these points is not a guide to the eye as for the two glasses, but it is an independent determination of τth​(T)\tau_{\rm th}(T) using the well-known kinetic expression for the thermal conductivity,

κ=13​Cv​vD2​τth.\kappa\;=\;{\scriptstyle\frac{1}{3}}\;C_{\rm v}v_{\rm D}^{2}\tau_{\rm th}\;\;. (15)

We observe that in this case the value of τth\tau_{\rm th} derived from κ\kappa (line) is in remarkable agreement with that obtained from the measurement of anharmonic damping of the acoustic modes. This emphasizes the physical significance of τth\tau_{\rm th}: it really is the mean lifetime of the excitations in the thermal bath which at sufficiently high TT is entirelly controlled by Umklapp (U) processes. As pointed out in [36], this produces a relaxation proportional to the phonon population, and thus at high TT one has τth∝T−1\tau_{\rm th}\propto T^{-1}. At intermediate TT, where Cv∝∼TC_{\rm v}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textstyle\sim}}{{\propto}}\;T and κ∝∼T−1\kappa\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textstyle\sim}}{{\propto}}\;T^{-1}, Eq. (15) indicates that τth∝T−2\tau_{\rm th}\propto T^{-2}. This is indeed observed in cc-SiO2 over a large range of TT, as seen in Fig.(6​b)\;(6b).

Equation (15) assumes propagating thermal phonons. For this reason, it becomes invalid in glasses at soon as TT increases beyond the thermal conductivity plateau located around 10 K in vv-SiO2. However, we remark that the functional dependence τth​(T)\tau_{\rm th}(T) observed in the two glasses is very similar in shape to that in cc-SiO2. We have no simple explanation for this. In glasses, there are two competing effects that modify the picture presented above. On the one hand, the strict quasi-momentum conservation which is invoqued in U-processes is strongly relaxed, and this must greatly enhance the interactions in the thermal bath, decreasing τth\tau_{\rm th}. This could account for the observed difference between crystal and glasses. On the other hand, the thermal modes are not expected to be propagating plane-waves but they are at best diffusive. This restricts the spatial extent of the modes, greatly decreasing their overlap and thereby their interactions, which increases τth\tau_{\rm th}. We believe it is the latter effect which produces the much longer τth\tau_{\rm th} in vv-SiO2 compared to dd-SiO2. Indeed, in dd-SiO2 the boson peak is strongly reduced [37]. This increases the crossover frequency ωco\omega_{\rm co} beyond which the acoustic excitations become diffusive, as recently confirmed by inelastic x-ray scattering [38]. This in turn increases the mean spatial extent of the modes and thereby their interactions leading to a faster thermalization.

Finally, we remark that the above analysis gives values for the mean Grüneisen parameter γ2\gamma^{2}. We find 0.95 for the LA-mode of x-cut quartz, 3.6 for vv-SiO2, and 8 for dd-SiO2. In the case of crystal quartz, the agreement between the line calculated from the thermal conductivity κ\kappa and that obtained from Q−1Q^{-1} gives a solid support for the value of γ2\gamma^{2}. Unfortunately, one cannot make a similar comparison for the glasses.

VI Summing-up

VI.1 The internal friction

Figure 7 summarizes the present analysis of the internal friction observed in vv-SiO2 with Brillouin scattering around 35 GHz. One identifies two main contributions: Qrel−1Q_{\rm rel}^{-1} arising from thermally activated relaxation and Qanh−1=Q−1−(Qrel−1+QTLS−1)Q_{\rm anh}^{-1}=Q^{-1}-(Q_{\rm rel}^{-1}+Q_{\rm TLS}^{-1}) which results from network viscosity. Around room TT, Qanh−1Q_{\rm anh}^{-1} is nearly twice as large as Qrel−1Q_{\rm rel}^{-1} . The incoherent tunneling contribution QTLS−1Q_{\rm TLS}^{-1}, if it really exists at these high frequency and temperatures, mainly produces the small hump around 40 K. Although there is a hint for such a feature in the data shown in Fig. 7, it would need to be confirmed by more precise measurements. Also, we neglected in this analysis a possible contribution arising from the quasi-harmonic oscillators of the soft-potential model [17]. This is explained in Appendix D.

As ν\nu is increased beyond 35 GHz, we find that the value Qrel−1Q_{\rm rel}^{-1} calculated with Eq. (9a) saturates. This saturation essentially results from the cut-off in f⁡(Δ)f(\Delta). For example at room TT, Qrel−1Q_{\rm rel}^{-1} does not increase beyond ∼\sim1.5×\times10-3. On the other hand, at sufficiently high TT, Qanh−1Q_{\rm anh}^{-1} continues to grow with Ω\Omega according to Qanh−1=A​Ω​τthQ_{\rm anh}^{-1}=A\Omega\tau_{\rm th} which applies as long as Ω​τth≪1\Omega\tau_{\rm th}\ll 1. We also find that A​τthA\tau_{\rm th} is practically constant from 100 to 300 K. For these reasons, the total Q−1Q^{-1} becomes dominated by network viscosity, it continues to increase proportionally to Ω\Omega up to several hundred GHz, and it is nearly TT-independent from 100 K to 300 K. This is in excellent agreement with the results on acoustic propagation reported for vv-SiO2 thin films by Zhu, Maris, and Tauc [39]. These authors find that the mean free path, ℓ−1\ell^{-1}, grows in Ω2\Omega^{2} from ∼\sim30 GHz to ∼\sim300 GHz, and that it is nearly independent of TT from 80 to 300 K. Since ℓ−1≡Q−1​Ω/v\ell^{-1}\equiv Q^{-1}\Omega/v, the dominance of Qanh−1Q_{\rm anh}^{-1}, its growth ∝Ω\propto\Omega, and its near constancy in TT, fully account for the data reported in [39]. Our predictions are also fully consistent with three data points measured with UV Brillouin scattering from ∼\sim50 to ∼\sim100 GHz [40, 41].

On the other hand, at ultrasonic frequencies, i.e. much below 35 GHz, the contribution of Qanh−1Q_{\rm anh}^{-1} which decreases proportionally to Ω\Omega becomes completely negligible compared to Qrel−1Q_{\rm rel}^{-1}. This justifies the analysis based only on TAR that was performed in relation with Fig. 1.

VI.2 The velocity changes

Figure(8​a)\;(8a) shows the velocity changes calculated from Eq.(9​b)\;(9b) for TAR, and using

(δ​vv)anh=−A2​11+Ω2​τth2\left(\frac{\delta v}{v}\right)_{\rm anh}\;=\;-\frac{A}{2}\;\frac{1}{1+\Omega^{2}\tau_{\rm th}^{2}}\;\; (16)

for the network viscosity, this at two typical frequencies. One notices that the increase in ν\nu from 6.8 MHz to 35 GHz leads to a large reduction of |δ​vrel||\delta v_{\rm rel}|. On the other hand, |δ​vanh||\delta v_{\rm anh}|, although quite large above 100 K, changes relatively little with ν\nu. In particular, the dashed curve is entirely in the regime Ω​τth≪1\Omega\tau_{\rm th}\ll 1, so that it is practically independent of Ω\Omega at lower Ω\Omega-values. This justifies the approach used to determine 𝒞{\cal C} in Fig. 2 where the anharmonicity contribution was simply neglected. At sufficiently high-TT, anharmonicity always leads to a quasi-linear decrease of vv with TT, very similar to what is observed in crystals [42, 43]. This has been seen in ultrasonic measurements in a large number of glasses, e.g. in [44] where this effect is interpreted as such. At these frequencies, one is in a regime where the velocity changes are dominated by network viscosity while the damping mainly originates from TAR. It is generally necessary to go up to Brillouin frequencies to observe in Q−1Q^{-1} both contributions simultaneously.

The velocity changes in tetrahedrally coordinated glasses, in particular in vv-SiO2 and in dd-SiO2, are more complex than described above. Fig.(8​b)\;(8b) shows the observed velocities, vv, and the unrelaxed value that is corrected for both TAR and network-viscosity dispersions, v∞=v−[(δ​v)rel+(δ​v)anh]v_{\infty}=v-[(\delta v)_{\rm rel}+(\delta v)_{\rm anh}]. As observed, the experimental points collapse to a v∞v_{\infty} which on this scale is essentially Ω\Omega-independent. However, rather than being constant, v∞v_{\infty} increases considerably with TT. In the same figure, the results obtained in (I) for dd-SiO2 are shown for comparison. Both solid lines are guides to the eye obtained by an ad hoc adjustment to Wachtman’s equation [45]. The behaviour of v∞v_{\infty} is remarkably similar in both glasses, pointing to an anomalous hardening of silica with increasing TT. As discussed in (I), the earlier proposal that this is a manifestation of large structural inhomogeneities [46] is not supported by observations. The anomalous hardening has recently been attributed to a progressive local polyamorphic transition associated with abrupt rotations of randomly distributed Si-O-Si bonds, found in simulations [47]. Thermal agitation would redistribute the Si-O-Si bond angles in configurations where they are more resilient. However, contrary to [48], our results indicate that a very similar mechanism would then be active in permanently densified silica. Repeating the warning made in (I), although v∞v_{\infty} has a clear physical significance, it would be nearly impossible to perform at the moment an experiment to directly measure it. This is even more so in vv-SiO2 than in dd-SiO2, owing to the lower ωco\omega_{\rm co} of the former glass.

VI.3 The tunneling strength

It remains to compare the value 𝒞=1.4×10−3{\cal C}=1.4\times 10^{-3} found in Section III to the tunneling-strength parameter C≃3.0×10−4C\simeq 3.0\times 10^{-4} from the literature. To do this, both values are inserted in Eq. (11) to calculate the cut-off energy WW that applies to the present case. We find W≃7W\simeq 7 K, as opposed to the TLS value W≃4W\simeq 4 K derived from the low-TT specific heat data [16]. Such a larger value of WW was already reported, resulting from a similar analysis in [18]. Its origin was convincingly explained there as arising from a different weighing of the distribution of WW-values, in W−4W^{-4} for the specific heat, and in W−1W^{-1} for the ultrasonic absorption. The value of 𝒞\cal C is thus fully in line with expectations.

VII Discussion

We have shown that ultrasonic and hypersonic damping and dispersion in vitreous silica at temperatures above the quantum regime originate in at least two main processes: thermally activated relaxation and network viscosity. These have different Ω\Omega and TT dependences which leads to a non-trivial variation of the scattering linewidth Γ\Gamma with Ω\Omega. At a given TT, TAR dominates the damping at low Ω\Omega, while anharmonicity dominates at sufficiently high Ω\Omega. Between these two regimes there occurs a “dynamical crossover” which for vv-SiO2 at room TT falls near our Brillouin frequency, as shown in Fig. 10 of [39] and confirmed in Fig. 7 above. Above this crossover, the damping is dominated by Qanh−1=A​Ω​τthQ_{\rm anh}^{-1}=A\Omega\tau_{\rm th}, which implies that Γ∝Ω2\Gamma\propto\Omega^{2}. As Ω\Omega is increased far beyond optical Brillouin frequencies, another broadening mechanism eventually comes into play. Around 300 GHz, one expects the onset of a new contribution to Q−1Q^{-1}, growing with a higher power of Ω\Omega, possibly in Ω3\Omega^{3}, as suggested in [49]. This additional contribution is currently thought to result from the hybridization of the acoustic modes with boson-peak excitations [50, 51], as inelastic x-ray scattering observations on dd-SiO2 strongly suggest [38, 52]. Unfortunately, inelastic x-ray scattering at sufficiently small scattering vectors and with sufficiently high energy resolution could not yet be performed on vv-SiO2 to settle the issue of this onset. This hybridization eventually leads to the Ioffe-Regel crossover at ωco\omega_{\rm co}, above which the excitations have lost their plane-wave character. Then, the wave-vector qq does not remain a good label for the modes which are at best diffusive [53]. The excitations of the thermal bath are expected to be of that nature in glasses, as discussed in Section V.

Power laws Γ∝Ωn\Gamma\propto\Omega^{n}, or Γ∝qn\Gamma\propto q^{n} which is equivalent as long as the frequency is well below the Ioffe-Regel limit so that q∝Ωq\propto\Omega, are often employed to represent the damping data Γ⁡(Ω)\Gamma(\Omega). As just explained, Γ∝Ω2\Gamma\propto\Omega^{2} is a reasonable approximation in the region between the dynamical crossover and the Ioffe-Regel one. On the opposite, such laws should be viewed as quite rough approximations in the TAR-dominated regime. The reason is that the dependence of Γ\Gamma on Ω\Omega predicted by Eq. 9a is more complicated. It cannot be written simply in terms of a TT-dependent exponent n⁡(T)n(T). For example, in vv-SiO2 at room TT, a value n=1.3n=1.3 is given in [54], while n=1.8n=1.8 is derived from [7]. We conclude that power laws in the TAR-dominated regime are ad hoc devices which only represent approximately the data, especially if the latter are sufficiently noisy to mask the disagreements.

At this point, it is legitimate to ask to what extent anharmonicity might be important to sound damping in other glasses. The answer to this question depends on two factors: i) the strength, density, and distribution of the relaxing defects; ii) the strength of the anharmonicity. It is conceivable that in glasses that contain a large quantity of defects up to high values of V0V_{0} and ΔC\Delta_{\rm C}, TAR would mask the anharmonicity. In that case the dynamical crossover might move up to nearly ωco\omega_{\rm co}, so that a regime Γ∝Ω2\Gamma\propto\Omega^{2} might not be observable at all. We have found such a case in lithium diborate, vv-Li2B4O7 [51]. This type of situation is expected for most polymers in which the tunneling strength CC is quite large [22]. On the other hand, there exist many glasses or amorphous materials for which CC is quite small, well below 10−410^{-4} [22]. Such are the amorphous group IV semiconductors, C, Si, and Ge. In that case, the anharmonicity is expected to dominate over a considerable range of Ω\Omega and a calculation to that effect has already been performed [55]. Of the tetrahedrally coordinated glasses, it will be particularly interesting to reinvestigate vv-GeO2 and vv-BeF2. Difficulties met in obtaining a quantitative description of damping and dispersion in germania on the basis of TAR alone, described in [10], might find their resolution by including in the analysis the cut-off ΔC\Delta_{\rm C} and the network-viscosity contribution.

To summarize, TAR essentially explains acoustic damping results in silica glass up to a few GHz. At higher frequencies, the anharmonic coupling of hypersound to the modes that form the entire thermal bath becomes progressively dominant. This conclusion, in line with previous observations [23] and simulations [55], corrects statements to the contrary often found in the literature, e.g. in [7, 8, 9]. The anharmonicity which in our view produces Qanh−1Q^{-1}_{\rm anh} is a coupling of sound to the whole bath, in addition to the relatively small fraction of modes forming the boson peak. This process, which we call network viscosity, is in a way quite similar to the usual lattice viscosity of crystals.

Appendix A Estimating Eqs. (9)

For the Marquardt-Levenberg adjustment of Eqs. (9), it is convenient to use the parameters 𝒞\cal C, V0V_{0}, logτ010{}_{10}\,\tau_{0}, ζ\zeta, and δ\delta. Taking as integration variable x≡V/V0x\equiv V/V_{0}, and defining the auxiliary variables α≡V0/T\alpha\equiv V_{0}/T and y≡Ω​τ0y\equiv\Omega\tau_{0}, Eq.(9​a)\;(9a) becomes

Qrel−1=𝒞​Φ​(2​δ/α)​α​∫0∞x−ζ​exp​(−12​x2)​y​exp​(α​x)1+y2​exp​(2​α​x)​𝑑x.Q_{\rm rel}^{-1}\;=\;{\cal C}\>\Phi(\sqrt{2}\,\delta/\alpha)\>\alpha\>\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{-\zeta}{\rm exp}(-{\scriptstyle\frac{1}{2}}\,x^{2})\;\frac{y\>{\rm exp}(\alpha x)}{1+y^{2}\>{\rm exp}(2\alpha x)}\>dx\;\;. (A​1)

Good results are obtained with a simple trapezoidal integration, taking a geometric progression for the vector of xx-values. We used xx starting at ≃10−4\simeq 10^{-4} and ending at ≃10\simeq 10, in steps of 1%. Eq.(9​b)\;(9b) is handled similarly.

Appendix B Velocity changes due to incoherent tunneling

One observes on the upper curves of Fig. 4 that there is a small difference in the high temperature slopes for the two different frequencies. The origin of this effect might be in the velocity dispersion associated, by the Kramers-Kronig transform, with the relatively small damping QTLS−1Q^{-1}_{\rm TLS} produced by incoherent tunneling. At high TT, the damping is given by the third equation (2.94) of [28],

QTLS−1=π​C4​rmin​ℏ​ΩkB​T.Q^{-1}_{\rm TLS}\;=\;\frac{\pi\,C}{4\,r_{\rm min}}\;\frac{\hbar\Omega}{k_{\rm B}T}\;\;. (B​1)

The corresponding δ​vTLS\delta v_{\rm TLS} is derived from the third equation (2.96) of [28], which gives for the Ω\Omega-dependent part

δ​vTLS≃ 0.45​CT∗​(ln​Ω)​T.\delta v_{\rm TLS}\;\simeq\;0.45\,\frac{C}{T^{*}}\;({\rm ln}\,\Omega)\,T\;\;. (B​2)

The temperature T∗T^{*} marks the end of the low-TT plateau region in Q−1Q^{-1} and it is given by Eqs. (2.78) and (2.79) of [28]. Owing to the logarithmic dependence in (B2), it is the difference of slopes at two frequencies which is significant,

Δ⁡(δ​vTLS)T≡(δ​v1)TLS−(δ​v2)TLST≃ 0.45​CT∗​ln​(Ω1/Ω2).\frac{\Delta(\delta v_{\rm TLS})}{T}\,\equiv\,\frac{(\delta v_{1})_{\rm TLS}-(\delta v_{2})_{\rm TLS}}{T}\simeq\,0.45\,\frac{C}{T^{*}}\,{\rm ln}\,(\Omega_{1}/\Omega_{2})\;. (B​3)

With the values in Fig. 4, and calculating T∗T^{*} following [28], one finds C≈7×10−5C\approx 7\times 10^{-5}. As expected, this is smaller than the tunneling strength found from specific heat measurements at low temperatures [22], the reduction being of the order of ΔC/T\Delta_{\rm C}/T. Hence, it is not unreasonable to assign the difference in slopes observed at high-TT in Fig. 4 to the Kramers-Kronig transform of QTLS−1Q^{-1}_{\rm TLS}.

Appendix C Solving Eq. (14) for the relaxation time

It is in principle trivial to solve the quadratic equation y=x/(1+x2)y=x/(1+x^{2}) for x≡Ω​τthx\equiv\Omega\tau_{\rm th} in terms of the measured y≡Q−1/Ay\equiv Q^{-1}/A. However, imaginary roots do occur in the region around x=1x=1 owing to fluctuations in the data leading to some points for which y>1/2y>1/2. These are the points whose ordinate lies above the maximum of the solid curve drawn in Fig.(6​a)\;(6a). For these data points, we simply replaced xx by 1, as the nearest real solution. This produces a line of data points with τth=1/Ω\tau_{\rm th}=1/\Omega in the presentation of Fig.(6​b)\;(6b). For the data points with y<1/2y<1/2, one must select between the upper and the lower root of the quadratic equation. This is set by the location of the maximum in the solid curve, TMaxT_{\rm Max}. For T<TMaxT<T_{\rm Max}, the upper root applies since Ω​τth>1\Omega\tau_{\rm th}>1, while the lower root applies at higher temperatures.

Appendix D Another possible source of damping

We have not considered the damping arising from the weak anharmonicity of the nearly harmonic oscillators (HO) of the soft potential model in the domain η>0\eta>0 [17]. This contribution should be most active at “intermediate” frequencies. In vv-SiO2, its strength has actually been predicted to be largest near our Brillouin frequency [17]. It must be noted that the entire (Ω,T)(\Omega,T)-domain covered by the propagating pulse measurements of [39] falls within this “intermediate” frequency range where the additional damping obeys QHO−1∝C​T/ΩQ^{-1}_{\rm HO}\propto CT/\sqrt{\Omega} [17]. If the strength of QHO−1Q^{-1}_{\rm HO} would be sufficient, one should definitely notice its effect on the (Ω,T)(\Omega,T)-dependence of the mean free path reported in [39] from 80 to 300 K and from 30 to 300 GHz. On the contrary, the mean free path is found practically TT-independent and it increases ∝Ω2\propto\Omega^{2}, in agreement with the network-viscosity contribution. It seems thus justified to neglect QHO−1Q^{-1}_{\rm HO} in our analysis of the Brillouin results up to 300 K. The difficulty in estimating the size of QHO−1Q^{-1}_{\rm HO} apparently lies in finding the proper value for the tunneling-strength parameter CC that applies to it. The value C=C= 3.0×\times10-4, appropriate for TLS at very low temperatures [22], is certainly too large here. Indeed, using this value in Eq. (3.18) of [17], we calculate QHO−1≃Q^{-1}_{\rm HO}\simeq 5×\times10−5×T{}^{-5}\times T(K), which at 300 K is larger than the entire Q−1Q^{-1} observed. ¿From an analysis of heat-release measurements there are grounds to adopt here a value of CC which is at least five times smaller [56]. Even so, the resulting QHO−1Q^{-1}_{\rm HO} is still too large to agree with the results of [39]. Our Brillouin measurements up to 700 K shown in Fig.(3​b)\;(3b) suggest that there could be a small contribution ∝T\propto T that starts being felt above ∼400\sim 400 K. This contribution would then be of the order of 10−6×T10^{-6}\times T(K), which implies a very small effective CC for this particular damping mechanism.
